newsitem.title: USA: U.S., EU end meat talks for day; no agreement yet.
newsitem.headline: U.S., EU end meat talks for day; no agreement yet.

text.p: U.S. and European Union officials ended negotiations Wednesday on a lingering dispute over meat import regulations without reaching any agreement, despite the pressure of a looming April 1 deadline.

Officials said there were no further meetings scheduled on the so-called veterinary equivalency rules, but that Washington would respond to an EU proposal for a "temporary solution" to the most contentious issues on Thursday.
"There's no deal yet," said U.S. Agriculture Department spokesman Jim Petterson. "We'll be analysing over the next couple of days what the next steps should be."
"It's fair to say we're still at it. There's been no conclusion," said EU spokesperson Ella Krucoff.

U.S. and EU negotiators have been meeting this week to resolve differences over meat import inspection rules before an approaching April 1 deadline threatens to disrupt hundreds of millions of dollars of meat, poultry, dairy and pet food trade between the two nations.
An agreement would allow each side to accept meat and meat products from the other even if the inspection methods differ.

The issue has been a bitter source of dispute between the two sides for years, and U.S. meat and poultry industry representatives have urged the Clinton administration to either solve the problem now, or to implement retaliatory action against the European Union.

Earlier Wednesday, EU's lead negotiator in the talks, Lars Hoelgaard, told reporters that the European Union has offered the United States a "temporary solution" for poultry import standards until a long-term solution can be worked out.
But a senior U.S. poultry industry official seemed sceptical.
Bill Roenigk, senior vice president of the National Broiler Council, said, "I'm not optimistic at this time ... I would be pleasantly surprised if they presented something to us we could accept."

Roenigk maintained that the EU refusal to accept U.S. poultry inspection methods is really an attempt to raise a non-tarriff trade barrier, and that U.S. poultry sales to Europe would be "several times" more than the current $50 million worth if the EU opened its markets.

The Agriculture Department's Petterson said the EU provided additional information on meat inspection requirements on Wednesday and that the agency would review the new material and decide on it by Thursday.
"We will be responding in writing to the additional information that was submitted," he said.
Krucoff said that although there are no further meetings scheduled at this point, the EU negotiators were staying in town and would be available for more talks if necessary.
Agriculture Department officials were expected to brief U.S. industry representatives on the talks sometime Thursday.
